rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence and turns gaps into reporting questions, not fake certainty. Its strongest move is "Rivian adds Tesla-style plugs and opens its network with no automaker partner in sight" because that is a real infrastructure/interoperability angle from the update. A has good bones, but "Rivian just became a charging-network operator. Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" invents market reaction the facts do not give us. That is how a decent angle set wanders into CNBC cosplay.
gaps_in_A: "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" is unsupported. No stock move, analyst note, or valuation evidence was in the update.
"After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs. The proprietary-charger era is fading." leans on external Tesla context and turns two examples into a trend without proof supplied.
The revenue angle and investor angle overlap: "whether this changes the business" versus "how Rivian should be valued" is a thin separation unless analyst evidence exists.
"move the needle" appears in the proof section. Small thing, but it is on the blacklist and it signals the writer briefly stopped choosing words.
gaps_in_B: "whether 'improves utilization' is a polite way of saying stalls sit empty" is sharp, but it flirts with implying underuse before Rivian gives a baseline.
"no automaker partner in sight" slightly overstates "no partnership announced." Keep it as a question unless Rivian confirms there is no deal.
It skips the investor-valuation angle entirely. That may be wise, but a markets reporter shape could still be useful if analyst reaction exists.
"funding-mechanics" is an odd story type label. The angle is really business-model economics; call it that and stop making the category work so hard.
